key_terms.meaning: Phase that takes the token stream from the lexer, checks it against the grammar, and builds a parse tree; it reports errors, it never guesses silently
A token sequence that no derivation of the grammar can produce, e.g. a missing ) or an operator with no right operand
Error strategy that throws away input tokens until one in a chosen synchronising set appears, then resumes parsing
Four-tuple G = (V, T, P, S): V nonterminals, T terminals, P productions A → α, S the start symbol
Sequence of rewrites starting at S and ending at a terminal string; leftmost derivation always rewrites the leftmost nonterminal
Tree whose root is S, interior nodes are nonterminals, leaves are terminals, and each node's children are the right side of the production used
Grammar in which some string has two different parse trees (equivalently, two leftmost derivations)
A production of the form A → Aα, which makes a top-down parser call itself forever
Rewriting A → αβ₁ | αβ₂ as A → αA′ , A′ → β₁ | β₂ so a parser can choose one production after seeing α
Top-down parser written as one procedure per nonterminal, each procedure trying the productions of that nonterminal in order
Undoing a production choice and trying the next one when the input does not match; needed only when the grammar is not predictive
Set of terminals that can begin a string derived from α; if α derives ε then ε is also in FIRST(α)
Set of terminals that can appear immediately after nonterminal A in some sentential form; $ is in FOLLOW(S)
Nonterminal that can derive ε, i.e. ε ∈ FIRST(A)
Grammar for which a one-token lookahead always decides the production, i.e. the table has at most one entry per cell
Two-dimensional array, rows are nonterminals, columns are terminals plus $, and entry M[A, a] is the production to expand A when the lookahead is a
Stack holding the start symbol at the bottom and $ on top; the top symbol drives each move
Terminal (usually from FOLLOW of the failing nonterminal) at which the parser discards input and continues
Error repair that inserts, deletes or replaces one token so parsing can continue locally
Any string of terminals and nonterminals reachable from the start symbol in zero or more derivation steps

takeaways: The parser turns a flat token stream into a tree and is the phase that reports syntax errors; it does not fix the program on its own.
A context-free grammar is a generating device, a derivation is one way it generates a string, and a parse tree is the record of that derivation.
Three rewrites make a grammar usable by a top-down parser: remove ambiguity, remove left recursion, apply left factoring.
A recursive descent parser is just code: one function per nonterminal, with a token pointer that only moves forward when the grammar is predictive.
FIRST tells you which production can start with the lookahead; FOLLOW tells you what may legally come next, and it is also what error recovery uses.
An LL(1) table entry M[A, a] = A → α means: with A on top of the stack and a as lookahead, replace A by α.
A cell with two productions proves the grammar is not LL(1); a cell that is empty is the moment a syntax error is detected.
Error recovery in predictive parsing is mechanical: report, then skip input until a token in FOLLOW(A) appears and pop A from the stack.
bank_note: Long answers here are almost always a full worked construction — clean up a given grammar, compute FIRST and FOLLOW, build the LL(1) table and then trace the parse of a sample string — so the syllabi reward showing every step with the table drawn, not just the final answer.

bank.q: Define a context-free grammar as a four-tuple. For the grammar E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → ( E ) | id, give a leftmost derivation and the corresponding parse tree for id + id * id.
outline: State G = (V, T, P, S) and name each component
Write the leftmost derivation step by step, always expanding the leftmost nonterminal
Draw the parse tree with the same structure; leaves read left to right give the input
Point out that the same string has only one leftmost derivation here, so this grammar is unambiguous

bank.q: Explain the role of the parser in a compiler and describe four general strategies for syntax error recovery.
outline: Parser obtains tokens from the lexer, verifies the grammar, builds the parse tree, passes it to the next phase
Detects and reports errors with line number; must recover to find further errors
Panic mode: skip tokens to a synchronising set
Phrase level: local repair by inserting or deleting a token
Error productions: grammar rules written to absorb common mistakes
Global correction: minimum-cost repair, rarely used in practice

bank.q: Explain ambiguity and left recursion in grammars. Why does a top-down parser fail on each, and how is each removed?
outline: Definition of ambiguous grammar: two parse trees for one string
Example grammar E → E + E | E * E | id and two trees for id + id * id
Precedence and associativity declarations or a layered grammar remove ambiguity
Definition of left recursion A → Aα | β
Elimination rule: A → βA′ , A′ → αA′ | ε
Show the rewritten grammar derives the same language

bank.q: Remove left recursion and apply left factoring to the grammar: S → i E t S | i E t S e S | a, E → b. Show the resulting grammar and state whether it is LL(1).
outline: Factoring the common prefix i E t S gives S → i E t S S′ | a, S′ → e S | ε
No left recursion is present, so only factoring is needed
Compute FIRST and FOLLOW of S, S′, E
Build the table and show no cell holds two productions, hence it is LL(1)
Mention that the original grammar is ambiguous for the dangling-else input

bank.q: For the grammar S → A a | b, A → b d | ε, compute FIRST and FOLLOW for every nonterminal.
outline: Mark A as nullable since A → ε
FIRST(A) = {b, ε}; FIRST(S) = {b, a}
FOLLOW(S) = {$}
FOLLOW(A) = {a} because A appears before terminal a in S → A a
Show the rules used for each set explicitly

bank.q: Construct the LL(1) predictive parsing table for a given grammar and trace the parse of the string id * id + id using the stack algorithm.
outline: Compute FIRST and FOLLOW, showing the sets
Place A → α in M[A, a] for each a in FIRST(α); for ε in FIRST(α) use each b in FOLLOW(A)
Draw the full table with rows nonterminals and columns terminals plus $
Write each move as (stack, input, action) triples
End when both stack and input hold $ and report acceptance

bank.q: Write a recursive descent parser in pseudo-code for a small expression grammar. State the FIRST sets that justify the order of the if-conditions in each procedure.
outline: One procedure per nonterminal: E(), T(), F()
Each procedure checks the lookahead token against FIRST of its alternatives
Include match(token) that advances the input pointer on success
Show error calls when no alternative matches
Explain that FIRST sets make backtracking unnecessary

bank.q: Show that the grammar S → S a | b is not LL(1), rewrite it, and rebuild the table to prove the new grammar is LL(1).
outline: Left recursion makes the table construction loop; S appears in FIRST(S a)
Apply A → βA′ , A′ → αA′ | ε to get S → b S′ , S′ → a S′ | ε
FOLLOW(S′) = {$}
Table cells M[S, b] and M[S′, a] and M[S′, $] are the only entries
Conclude one entry per cell, so LL(1)

bank.q: A predictive parser finds M[A, a] empty. Explain, with an example trace, how FOLLOW-based synchronisation and token deletion let parsing continue and report more than one error.
outline: Empty cell means the lookahead cannot start any production of A
Panic-mode recovery: report the error, then discard input tokens until one is in FOLLOW(A)
Then pop A from the stack and resume
Alternative: if a is in FIRST of some production of A, push a dummy symbol or skip the token
Show a trace with two errors to prove parsing restarts and reports both
Mention the risk of endless loops and how popping A avoids it

bank.q: Compare recursive descent parsing with table-driven LL(1) parsing: structure, memory use, speed, error handling and grammar restrictions.
outline: Recursive descent: code per nonterminal, uses the call stack, easy to debug and to attach semantic actions
Table-driven: one loop plus an explicit stack and a table, table size is |V| × (|T|+1)
Both need LL(1) grammar, hence no left recursion and no common prefixes
Recursive descent can backtrack on non-LL(1) grammars; LL(1) cannot
Error reporting is usually better in hand-written recursive descent because line context is known
Table size can be compressed but the loop is slightly slower per token

bank.q: Given a grammar for a small language, carry out the full top-down pipeline: remove ambiguity, remove left recursion, left factor, compute FIRST and FOLLOW, build the LL(1) table, and state every conflict you meet.
outline: Original grammar listed and its ambiguity or left recursion identified
Step-by-step rewrites with reasons
FIRST and FOLLOW table for every nonterminal
LL(1) table drawn completely
Conflicts, if any, named by their cell and the two competing productions
Conclusion: grammar is LL(1) or a further rewrite is needed

bank.q: Why can no LL(1) parser handle a left-recursive grammar or a grammar with a common prefix? What are the limits of LL(1) compared with LR parsing?
outline: Left recursion means A is in FIRST(Aα), so M[A, a] gets two entries
Common prefix makes FIRST(αβ₁) and FIRST(αβ₂) overlap
LL(1) uses one token of lookahead and never looks at the stack below the top
LL(1) cannot handle left-associative operators without rewriting
LR parsers postpone the decision and accept a larger class of grammars
LL(k) with k>1 or LR(1) costs more table space

bank.q: A student claims that if a grammar is left-factored it must be LL(1). Test this claim with a counterexample and say what extra condition is really needed.
outline: Left factoring only removes common prefixes of alternatives of the same nonterminal
It does not remove ambiguity or left recursion
Counterexample: a grammar whose FIRST/FOLLOW sets still overlap, or an ambiguous grammar that is already factored
Real condition: for every A and every pair of distinct productions, FIRST sets are disjoint, and if one derives ε then FIRST of the other does not meet FOLLOW(A)
Conclude that factoring is necessary but not sufficient

bank.q: Design the syntax error handling of a predictive parser for a small language and justify each choice: which synchronising sets, when to pop, when to skip a token, and how to avoid reporting one mistake many times.
outline: Use FOLLOW(A) as the primary synchronising set
Skip input tokens until one is in FOLLOW(A), then pop A
Use FIRST of A to decide whether a token can be deleted
Report each error once, with line number and the expected token set
Avoid cascading errors by not reporting again until a token is successfully consumed
Mention phrase-level repair as a refinement for missing semicolons

glossary.def: Classified unit of input such as id, number or the keyword if, produced by the lexer and consumed by the parser.
Symbol that appears in the input string itself, written in a grammar as a literal or a token class.
Grammar symbol that must be rewritten by a production before it can become terminals.
Rule of the form A → α saying nonterminal A may be replaced by the string α.
The designated nonterminal from which every derivation begins.
Any string of terminals and nonterminals reachable from the start symbol in zero or more steps.
Derivation in which the leftmost nonterminal is always the one rewritten next.
Ordered tree whose yield is the input string and whose internal nodes record the productions used.
Grammar in which at least one string has two distinct parse trees.
Production A → Aα in which the nonterminal is the first symbol on its own right side.
Delaying the choice between alternatives that share a prefix by pushing the common part out and choosing later.
For a string α, the set of terminals that can begin a string derived from α, plus ε if α derives ε.
For a nonterminal A, the set of terminals that can appear immediately to the right of A in some sentential form.
A nonterminal A is nullable when A ⇒ ε in one or more steps.
Top-down parsing in which the next production is chosen from the lookahead token alone, with no backtracking.
Grammar readable left to right, producing a leftmost derivation, with one token of lookahead.
Array M[A, a] giving the production to use when nonterminal A is on top of the stack and a is the lookahead.
The next input token the parser examines without consuming it.
Set of tokens, usually FOLLOW(A), at which the parser may discard input and resume parsing.
Recovery that abandons the current construct and skips input until a safe token appears.
Recovery that performs a small local repair such as inserting a missing semicolon or deleting a stray token.
Classic ambiguity where an else can attach to either of two nested if statements.
Retrying an earlier production choice after a mismatch; predictive parsers avoid it entirely.
Parser written as mutually recursive procedures, one for each nonterminal.
